chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdullah from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Ja'far ibn Bashir from 'Umar ibn Yazid said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Adhan (call to prayer) without the Iqamah (second call) in the Maghrib prayer, so he said, 'There is no harm in it, and I dislike that it be made a habit.' Thus, it is not contradictory to what we mentioned, because he only permitted restricting oneself to the Iqamah in this prayer in the presence of an incident or a preventer, then he drew his attention with his saying, 'And I dislike that it be made a habit.' This is on the condition that the preferred action is to do so, and that which reveals what we mentioned, that he only permitted restricting oneself to the Iqamah in all other prayers for an incident or a preventer, is what he narrated:

key_terms.الإِقَامَة: Iqamah (the second call to prayer, recited immediately before standing for prayer)
key_terms.الاِقْتِصَار: Restriction or limiting oneself to (doing only what is necessary)
key_terms.مَانِع: Preventer or obstacle (a reason that prevents the full ritual)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to skip the Adhan and only perform the Iqamah for Maghrib prayer?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Ja'far ibn Bishr reports that Imam al-Sadiq (AS) permitted omitting the Adhan for Maghrib prayer in favor of the Iqamah when a valid excuse (*'arid*) exists, such as urgency or fear. The Imam's addition, 'and I dislike that it be made a habit,' establishes a hierarchy of preference (*istihbab*), distinguishing between the permissibility of the exception and the superiority of the full ritual. This ruling serves as a foundational evidence for the flexibility of prayer rituals in Shia jurisprudence, allowing for the Iqamah-only practice in other prayers under similar conditions of necessity.
